source: Wang et al. (2026) GAVEL: Graph World Models for Verified and Efficient Long-Horizon LLM Task Planning
finding: An explicit graph world model (objects, relations, action preconditions and effects) rolls the LLM's plan forward, finds invalid steps, and repairs them. This lifts success even for frontier models, so the benefit does not vanish with model strength in this setting.
numbers: BEHAVIOR-1K, 100-instruction multi-task subset. Without GAVEL: Qwen3-4B 2.4, Qwen3-8B 23.6, GPT-5.6 Sol 24.6, Claude Sonnet 5 38.6 percent. With GAVEL: 75.2, 89.2, 99.2, 99.4 percent. Planning time for Sonnet 5: 18.0 s vs 18.2 s.
quote: Scaling alone improves semantic planning but does not eliminate long-horizon failures.
limits: Symbolic simulator, not geometric. The graph is built from known action definitions, not written by the LLM. The comparison is LLM alone vs LLM plus verifier, so it is a verify-and-repair gain, not a map-in-the-prompt gain. Tokens not matched. Preprint.
agent_relevance: For a strong model, a checked transition model outside the prompt helps a lot. Supports S2 plus a verify step, but the verifier must be code or a real checker, not the model reviewing itself.

source: Wang et al. (2026) GAVEL, Experiments 1 and 2 (repair vs feedback replanning)
finding: Returning failures to the LLM for replanning (SayPlan style) is weaker and costlier than repairing the plan from the graph model. Graph repair alone beats feedback-only replanning on a 4B model with one query instead of 3.4.
numbers: Exp 1 (100 single tasks): Qwen3-4B llm-only 21.8, SayPlan-style 55.4 (3.4 LLM calls), graph repair only 67.7, full GAVEL 88.8 (1.7 calls). Qwen3-8B: 41.2, 76.4 (2.7 calls), 76.2, 91.8 (1.5 calls). Exp 2 (500 multi-task, Qwen3-8B): llm-only 19.9, SayPlan 75.6, graph-only (EPoG-style) 60.2, GAVEL 92.6, oracle 100. Of 38 residual failures, 21 were object extraction, 5 unexecutable, 9 unmet goals.
limits: Small models in Exp 1 and 2. The graph-only baseline fails exactly on tasks needing appliance-induced states (graph difference cannot say run the dishwasher). Symbolic world, so a changed transition is a replanning event the verifier detects, not a human-style detour.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 6: a re-plan step that uses the map to repair beats asking the model again. Keep the LLM for semantic gaps and use the map for legality.

source: Song and Cai (2026) Agentic vs. Parametric World Models: Hybrid Planning for Reliable Language Agents (Hybrid-WM)
finding: On four graph-structured planning benchmarks, the language agent's own imagined state changes contain many hallucinated node states. A small learned transition model that checks each imagined step cuts hallucination and raises success. Chain of thought beat direct prompting; a separate verifier cut invalid actions but barely cut hallucinated states.
numbers: Averaged over 8 seeds (success, hallucinated-state rate): Agent-Direct 0.496 / 0.252; Agent-CoT 0.591 / 0.225; Agent-Replan 0.668 / 0.205; Agent-Verifier 0.684 / 0.193 (invalid-action rate 0.062); Hybrid-WM 0.838 / 0.079. Tokens per success: CoT 21301, Replan 16389, Hybrid-WM 15021 (fewer than CoT).
limits: Mostly simulated benchmarks; one table notes only the GPT-4o-mini TaskGraph result used live inference. Backbones are weak or mid (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Haiku, Gemini-1.5-Flash, Llama-3-8B). The parametric model is trained, which a prompt-only agent does not have.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 in part: an unverified self-imagined state model is wrong on about 19 to 25 percent of node states even with replanning. Checking against ground truth, not self-review, is what reduces it.

source: Song and Cai (2026) Hybrid-WM, Table 6 backbone comparison
finding: The hallucinated-state rate of the agent's own world model rises as the backbone gets weaker, and grounding gives the biggest gain for the weakest model. The gain shrinks with model strength.
numbers: Agent vs Hybrid-WM success (hallucinated-state rate): GPT-4o-mini 75.5 to 79.5 (17.1 to 1.4); Claude-3-Haiku 62.0 to 79.0 (20.4 to 7.4); Gemini-1.5-Flash 60.0 to 78.0 (23.1 to 8.8); Llama-3-8B 47.0 to 73.0 (31.8 to 10.9). Structured-output format error: 0.4, 3.2, 4.0, 9.2 percent.
limits: Gain is +4 points for the strongest tested model vs +26 for the weakest. No frontier or reasoning model tested. Cost per 1k tasks rose from 0.74 to 1.06 dollars for GPT-4o-mini.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 in direction: the benefit of a grounded map falls with model strength (+26 to +4 across four models) but is not zero at the top of this range. Structured-format failures are a real cost for weak models.

source: Li et al. (2026) GraphThink: Graph-Enhanced LLM Thinking for Long-Horizon Embodied Task Planning
finding: A task graph (subtasks as nodes, precondition-compatible transitions as edges) goes in the prompt, graph-edge rewards are used in GRPO training, and a graph verifier runs at inference. The ablation shows most gain comes from training, then the graph in the prompt, with the verifier adding a little.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ALFRED-style splits (Valid Seen / Valid Unseen / Long Horizon success percent): full 96.22 / 96.56 / 90.04; without task-graph prompt 77.93 / 74.11 / 40.69; without GRPO 49.88 / 52.64 / 33.67; without verification 95.12 / 95.09 / 86.25.
limits: The prompt ablation is applied to a model trained with the graph, so the prompt-only effect is not isolated. 7B model, trained. Success is by a plan checker in a simulator.
agent_relevance: A prompted task graph helps a trained 7B model; the verifier adds only 1 to 4 points. For a frozen strong model only the prompt part is usable, and its stand-alone effect is untested here.

source: Kim et al. (2024) Cognitive maps paper (arXiv 2406.15275), few-shot appendix E.2, Tables 8-10
finding: Closes gap 10 for prompting: with 0 to 4 demonstrations, no model produced useful output when told to write a cognitive map before planning on textual gridworlds. The only model that did well was o1 with no special prompt.
numbers: 100 Textualized Gridworld samples, 4 demos. NONE prompt, o1: 0, 18, 34, 38 percent for 0/1/2/4-shot; Llama-3 8B, 70B and GPT-4o: 0 percent at all shots. COT prompt: o1 0, 0, 10, 0; GPT-4o at most 1. COGNITIVE MAP prompt: o1 0, 0, 0, 10; GPT-4o 0, 1, 0, 1.
quote: None of the tested foundation models could produce meaningful results for the cognitive map approach through few-shot prompting
limits: The PDF table layout is interleaved; model-row assignment is by row order and consistent with the text claim 'up to 38% with 4-shot'. Only 4 demos, one task family. o1 tested in 2024.
agent_relevance: Explicit-map prompting did worse than no map prompt for a reasoning model (10 vs 38 percent at 4-shot). Do not assume a written map beats a strong reasoner's own reasoning. Few-shot did not transfer the benefit; many-shot untested.

source: Wu, Zhao, Chen (2026) When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Cross-family audit of neuroscience parallels in LLMs
finding: Audit of four brain-like findings in 17 open models (0.6B to 72B, five families). The linear world map (Gurnee and Tegmark style) is the only parallel that survives every control; concept steering, number-line neurons and language localisation depend on measurement choices.
numbers: World map: ridge probes on held-out cities recover latitude and longitude with R2 0.43 to 0.68 in all 17 models, near zero with shuffled labels; Qwen3-1.7B R2 0.62 latitude and 0.66 longitude. Concept steering looks scale-dependent with raw units but shows no significant trend with residual-norm-matched, held-out settings.
limits: Decoding only: shows information is present, not that the model uses it. Tests cities, not task graphs.
agent_relevance: Space in activations replicates widely, so an LLM can hold coordinates internally, but that says nothing about whether writing a map into the context helps. Do not use steering-style map claims as evidence.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) Mind over Space: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Mentally Navigate? (Video2Mental, NavMind)
finding: Frontier multimodal models cannot build usable cognitive maps from long egocentric video and plan landmark paths from them. A fine-tuned 8B model that writes a hierarchical map first does much better, and the hierarchical map beat a flat grid map.
numbers: Average planning success across evaluated models: 5.54 percent (target) and 3.76 percent (path). Predicted-map quality: landmark mean IoU below 5 percent, landmark F1 under 35 percent. Frontier models include GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3-Pro. Path success drops about 2.1 points from middle to long range even with a ground-truth map.
limits: Video input, not text graphs. The big gain is from supervised fine-tuning (Qwen3-VL-8B), not prompting. I did not read the ablation figure values; the hierarchical-vs-flat claim is from the text only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: models' own maps built from perception are poor, so a written map needs a check. Gap 4: a hierarchical map format beat a flat grid format, but in a trained model.

source: Kransberg et al. (2026) Failure to detect entorhinal grid-like signals in a passive navigation human fMRI study. Imaging Neuroscience
finding: A pre-registered, large fMRI sample finds no 6-fold grid-like signal in entorhinal cortex during passive virtual navigation. Bayes factors favour the null but are partly insensitive.
numbers: N=110 primary (207 exploratory). 6-fold right EC t(109)=0.728, p=0.234, BF01=7.31, d=0.07; left EC t(109)=-0.443, p=0.671, BF01=8.60. Younger (n=80) right EC t(79)=1.5, p=0.068, BF01=2.76. Temporal stability 50.78 percent, p=0.121. Spatial stability about half of participants vs 81 percent in Doeller 2010.
limits: Spatial task, passive movement, only 3 to 4 trials per direction bin, 2.6 mm voxels, whole-EC mask; authors list these as reasons for a weak test. Not a test of abstract conceptual space, so it does not refute the conceptual result directly. Agrees with a 2024 passive null and a 2023 study seeing 6-fold in observation but not self-navigation.
agent_relevance: The grid-like fMRI code is context dependent and fragile. Keep it out of the schema; S2 should not cite hexagonal coding as evidence.

source: Theves, Fernandez, Doeller (2020) Distance and direction codes underlie navigation of a novel semantic space in the human brain. J Neurosci
finding: Partial conceptual replication of a grid-like code for an abstract 2-D space: a 6-fold effect appears in right entorhinal cortex after learning, but not in mPFC, and the pre- versus post-learning contrast is only marginal.
numbers: N=25. Right EC searchlight peak p<0.005, small-volume corrected p<0.05. mPFC 6-fold t(24)=0.41, p=0.68. Pre-learning 6-fold t(24)=-0.55, p=0.58; post minus pre t(24)=1.89, p=0.07. Controls: 4-fold t(24)=0.35; 5-fold t(24)=-2.37, p=0.02; 7-fold t(24)=-2.14, p=0.04. Entorhinal distance code t(24)=2.14, one-tailed p=0.02.
limits: Only 8 movement directions sampled; 2-fold symmetry not excluded; negative 5- and 7-fold effects complicate reading. Small N and small-volume correction.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a second positive but weak replication. Unlike the original, mPFC was null here.

source: Park, Miller, Boorman (2021) Inferences on a multidimensional social hierarchy use a grid-like code. Nat Neurosci
finding: A 6-fold grid-like signal appears in entorhinal cortex and mPFC when people infer relations on an abstract 2-D social hierarchy, and it recurs when the grid angle is estimated from a session more than a week earlier.
numbers: N=21 analysed (25 scanned; only 39 of 92 who finished day 2 passed the behaviour threshold). EC peak MNI [22,-10,-28], t=4.11, TFCE p<0.05 within ROI; mPFC peak t=4.72. 4-, 5-, 7- and 8-fold controls all p>0.05 and 6-fold stronger than each. Accuracy at ceiling, 98.68 percent.
limits: Small N with heavy selection by training performance. Authors note TPJ, STS and dorsal mPFC effects could be theory-of-mind rather than grid cells; linear vs nonlinear geometry unresolved; only 2 of 21 reported a 2-D mental picture.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the most convincing positive abstract-space replication (cross-day stability), but still N=21 and selected. No source found reaches N above 30 for conceptual grid coding.

source: Baram, Muller, Nili, Garvert, Behrens (2021) Entorhinal and ventromedial prefrontal cortices abstract and generalize the structure of reinforcement learning problems. Neuron
finding: People transfer the abstract structure of an RL problem to new stimuli, and right entorhinal cortex carries a structure code independent of stimulus identity. The paper did not measure hexagonal grid-like signals and says so.
numbers: Final N=28 of 49 trained (17 failed training criteria, 4 scan exclusions). Within- vs across-structure cross-validation t(27)=9.54, p<1e-9; vs naive model t(27)=4.29, p=0.0002. Right EC searchlight p=0.005 small-volume (Bonferroni 0.01); left EC p=0.73. vmPFC prediction-error by structure interaction uncorrected p=0.014 left, 0.02 right.
limits: Modest N after heavy exclusion; multivariate vmPFC test uncorrected; hemisphere difference post hoc; structure and naive regressors correlated (r=0.77 for values, 0.93 for prediction errors).
agent_relevance: Behavioural transfer of relational structure is strong; the neural story is weaker. Supports reusing a structure template across tasks, not grid geometry.

source: Baram et al. (2026) An abstract relational map emerges in the human medial prefrontal cortex with consolidation. Current Biology
finding: An abstract, stimulus-independent graph code appears in mPFC only in the second scan after consolidation, not in the first. Entorhinal cortex shows no emergent cross-graph effect. Grid-like coding was not measured.
numbers: N=22 analysed (23 recruited), two graphs with the same 17-node structure. Cross-graph suppression whole-brain cluster p=0.003, peak t(21)=5.1, MNI [2,42,8]. Session 2 minus session 1 t(21)=2.56, p=0.02, dz=0.55. EC p=0.204. Overlap with an earlier grid-like mPFC region t(21)=2.38, p=0.03, called speculative.
limits: Small N; scans 1 to 7 days apart; consolidation not separated from extra exposure; sleep and replay not tested.
agent_relevance: Humans build the abstract relational map slowly (days), not within one session. A within-context map in an LLM is a different thing; do not read neural consolidation as support for in-prompt maps.

source: Lan, Hunt, Summerfield (2025) Goal-directed navigation in humans and deep reinforcement learning agents relies on an adaptive mix of vector-based and transition-based strategies. PLoS Biology
finding: Humans in new 8x8 grids use both a geometric (vector) and a topological (state-transition) map, mostly heading by vector and switching to transitions near landmarks, goals and obstacles. Deep RL agents show a similar mix. Cluttered grids hurt the vector-only condition more.
numbers: N=401 humans in 3 experiments (Exp1 200, Exp2 100, Exp3 about 200 before exclusions); 20 RL agents. Humans chose directions on 73.8 percent of steps in open grids and 63.6 percent in cluttered grids; agents 73.2 percent. Worst performance when only states were allowed, best when both. Landmark number had no effect (log Bayes factor -27.39 for the null).
limits: Online volunteers aged 18 to 40; stylised grids; detours not a separate condition (boulders only block adjacent moves). Agents showed no grid-cell-like units.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 by analogy: a useful map offers both a direction/coordinate view and an adjacency view; neither alone is best. Not an LLM test.

source: Qin, Cohen, Reddy (2026) Cognitive Maps in Large Language Models (re-opened for format reading)
finding: Open-weight models above about 10B parameters infer unstated relations and generalise to synthetic names. Relations are stored as pairwise links composed when queried, not as positions in a global coordinate system. Binding runs through a sparse set of key-value pairs; editing them plants false memories.
numbers: Abstract-level claims re-read in the PDF; about 1 percent of key-value pairs suffice for binding. The supplement has a section on query format (section VII) that I did not read in detail.
quote: Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried
limits: Mechanistic, open-weight models, family-tree-type tasks, not a prompt-format comparison. No test of an explicitly written map.
agent_relevance: Suggests the natural in-context format is a list of pairwise relations (edges) that the model composes at query time. No direct format comparison exists yet; this is the best prior.

source: Kim et al. (2024) Cognitive maps paper (arXiv 2406.15275), appendix E.3: trained map vs trained DFS exploration
finding: Even when trained, a plain depth-first-search trace beats the written cognitive map on success, while the map is more efficient in steps. A map is a cost-saver, not an accuracy-saver, once search is allowed.
numbers: Success: DFS-trained 94.5 percent vs cognitive-map 88.5 percent. Steps: map grows near-linearly with optimal path length; DFS grows quadratically.
limits: Small gridworld, trained models, one paper.
agent_relevance: With enough token budget, search with backtracking is as good or better than a written map. Compare any map against equal-token search (gap 1).
